results.title: In summary, whether the two channels are substitutive or complementary depends on the customer’s demand states. Consumers under a demand formation state manifest a complementary relationship between recommendation and search. In addition, the complementary effect is likely to be observed as irrelevant to customers’ previous interests, as recommended products can inform a customer of products with which she is not usually familiar. On the other hand, in the demand fulfillment state, product recommendations can reduce search costs and function as a substitute for customer search (Adomavicius and Tuzhilin 2005, De et al. 2010, Brynjolfsson et al. 2011, Adomavicius et al. 2018). We expect that the substitution effect will appear only when customers see fewer products of interest in the recommendation system. In this context, they must search significantly further to fulfill their demands. Shocker (1991) also states that an individual's final consideration set reflects subjective characteristics related to her attitudes and perceptions, emphasizing the important role of customers’ prior interests in the shopping process.

item.text: {"text":"Recent work separates recurring intent from immediate demand. [HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/) combines latent intent clustering, Hawkes processes for recurring interests, and attention for short-term adaptation. [TSRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08531) models user-specific repeat intervals, item-specific intervals, and similarity to previous repeat sequences. These support learning when interests recur, but do not establish that an interaction leaves a need unsatisfied. [TALE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07382) offers a cheaper starting point: temporal weighting of item transitions and normalization for changing popularity.\n\nComplementarity and substitution depend on context: controlled experiments found interactions between recommendation type and purchase decision stage, challenging a single similarity-based relevance score. This evidence predates the requested period and does not identify satisfaction from interaction logs. ([Zhang and Bockstedt, 2020](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378720620302792)) Practical hypothesis for this benchmark: augment SASRec with a small elapsed-time-conditioned gate over persistent preference, recent intent, and directed item transitions; optionally test temporary suppression of close semantic neighbors after an interaction, with learned recovery over time. Titles/descriptions can supply text similarity without pretrained weights; training histories supply transition evidence. Treat these as predictive proxies, never observed complement/substitute or satisfaction labels. Because simulator recommendations exclude seen items, exact-item repeat models need adaptation to recurring semantic interests. Use only timestamps available at prediction; if query time is absent, avoid target-time leakage. Select through the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10."}
